reading.title: How Writers Build Tone
reading.purpose: See how word choice and sentence patterns make a writer's attitude easy to hear.
paras: When you talk with a friend, your voice carries information that the words alone do not. A flat voice, a rising voice, or a long pause can change what "fine" means. Writers have no voice to use, so they build tone through other choices. Tone is the attitude a writer takes toward a subject, and readers can learn to hear it.

Word choice is the strongest signal. A writer who calls an empty house "quiet" sounds neutral. One who calls it "hollow" and mentions old photographs may sound wistful, gently longing for days that are gone. Someone who calls the same place "just a building" is probably indifferent, which means the writer shows no care either way. A solemn tone uses formal words and short, weighty sentences, as in a speech at a memorial. A whimsical tone does the opposite and plays with odd comparisons, such as calling a thunderstorm "the sky moving its furniture."

Sentence patterns matter too. Sarcastic writers say the opposite of what they mean. If a review says, "What a thrilling two hours of waiting," the praise is a mask for mockery. A cynical writer goes further and doubts people's motives. He might claim that every free gift hides a price. An irreverent writer pokes fun at things others treat as important, such as a famous rule or a famous person. An earnest writer does the reverse and writes plainly, with deep feeling and real effort behind each line.

Tone can also be mixed. A poem about autumn may be melancholy, sad in a quiet, lasting way without naming one cause. A letter written before a big move may sound apprehensive and wistful at once, because the writer worries about what may happen soon while missing what is left behind. To find the tone, ask three questions. Which words carry feeling? Does the writer mean what the sentence literally says? What does the writer want me to feel? Then answer with evidence from the text, not a guess.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "indifferent" most nearly means
choices: mocking something by saying the opposite
showing no care about the subject
treating the subject with great formality
qs.why: The text restates it right away: an indifferent writer "shows no care either way."

qs.q: Which sentence gives an example of sarcasm?
choices: A flat voice, a rising voice, or a long pause can change what "fine" means.
A whimsical tone does the opposite and plays with odd comparisons, such as calling a thunderstorm "the sky moving its furniture."
He might claim that every free gift hides a price.
If a review says, "What a thrilling two hours of waiting," the praise is a mask for mockery.
qs.why: The review praises something that was clearly dull, so the words mean the opposite of what the writer thinks.

ev.text: If a review says, "What a thrilling two hours of waiting," the praise is a mask for mockery.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Readers should guess a writer's tone from the title alone and then ignore every word that follows it.
Every piece of writing keeps exactly one tone from its very first line to its very last line.
Writers show attitude with word choice and sentence patterns, and readers can prove it.
Sarcasm and irreverence are the two most common tones in nearly every text a student will ever read.
qs.why: The reading explains how word choice and sentence patterns signal tone, and it ends by telling readers to answer with evidence.

qs.q: A writer claims that every free gift hides a price. Which tone does this most likely show?
qs.why: The reading says a cynical writer doubts people's motives, and expecting a hidden price behind a gift is exactly that.
